To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the attentional costs of anti-phase bimanually coordinated movements are largely associated with the frontal attentional system and are not associated with the posterior attentional system.
visual task difficulty and coordination mode have differential effects on reaction time, accuracy and electrophysiology during dual-task performance.
the attentional load associated with bimanual coordination and the difficulty of a concurrent visual task are reflected by changes in P3b and/or P3a amplitude.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of dual-task performance and the effect that bimanual coordination has on the ability to process visual stimuli.
understanding how visual task difficulty and coordination mode influence dual-task performance, and the electrophysiological mechanisms that underpin these behavioural effects.
the effects of visual task and bimanual motor task difficulty and coordination mode on behavioural and electrophysiologic measures of dual-task performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the attentional load of the bimanual coordination tasks is not the same for all participants.

the behavioural and electrophysiologically observed differences between the in-phase and anti-phase coordination conditions for the easy visual task are likely due to the increased attentional demand required for maintaining the anti-phase coordination pattern.
the attentional load associated with anti-phase coordination is not as large as that associated with the more difficult visual task, but is greater than that associated with in-phase coordination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the frontal attentional system is responsible for maintaining the bimanual coordination pattern and the posterior attentional system for the processing of the visual task.
the attentional costs associated with the coordination of bimanual movement are dependent on the difficulty of the visual task and the coordination mode.
, for the easy visual task under the anti-phase condition, participants are able to use the automaticity of the bimanual coordination system to facilitate the performance of the visual task.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cost of anti-phase bimanua coordination is not due to an increase in attentional resources required for the maintenance of the bimanual coordination but instead to a reduction in attentional resources available for the visual task.
the difficulty of a visual task can be modulated by varying the discrimination difficulty of stimuli and the coordination mode between the two hands.
the difficulty of a visual task can be dissociated from the difficulty of a bimanual task, and that these two types of difficulty interact in a complex manner.
